summary: Describes a one-time password system for login and other uses that is secure against passive attacks based on replaying captured reusable passwords. It is an Internet standard and replaces RFC 1938.

plainLanguage.summary: The One-Time Password system gives a user a sequence of login codes derived from a secret pass-phrase. Each accepted code is different, so someone who captures one cannot replay it to authenticate again.

questions: what is a one-time password system
how does otp s/key authentication work
how does otp prevent replay attacks
subtitle: A one-time password sequence designed to make captured login codes unusable for replay.

tldr.problem: An eavesdropper can capture a reusable password sent over a network and replay it later to gain access.
tldr.mechanism: The client derives a sequence of one-time passwords from a secret pass-phrase and a server-supplied seed. The server checks each new password by hashing it once and comparing the result with the previously accepted password.
tldr.outcome: The pass-phrase does not need to cross the network during authentication, but the system does not protect data privacy or prevent active attacks such as session hijacking. RFC 2289 obsoletes RFC 1938.

today: RFC 2289 is an Internet Standard published in February 1998. It obsoletes RFC 1938.

sections.title: Preventing Reuse of Captured Passwords
sections.content:
RFC 2289 describes a one-time password (OTP) system for logins and other authentication uses. It is designed to resist passive replay attacks, in which an eavesdropper records a reusable password and later presents it to gain access.

The user keeps a secret pass-phrase. A generator uses the pass-phrase and a challenge from the server to produce a one-time password. The server verifies the password, records the last valid value and its sequence number, and supports secure reinitialization of the pass-phrase sequence.

The pass-phrase never needs to cross the network during authentication or pass-phrase changes. The RFC also says that no secret information needs to be stored on any system, including the protected server.
sections.plainLanguage: The user does not send the secret pass-phrase to the server. Instead, the generator produces a different login code for each step in the sequence.

sections.title: Hash Functions and Password Size
sections.content:
OTP relies on a secure hash function that is practical to compute but computationally infeasible to reverse. The RFC defines interfaces for MD4, MD5 and SHA. A conforming server and generator must support MD5, should support SHA and may support MD4. Both ends need to use the same algorithm.

The hash output is folded to 64 bits. That 64-bit value is the one-time password, which the RFC describes as short enough to enter manually when necessary. Appendix A specifies how the output is folded and requires hash output to be represented in little-endian order before folding.
sections.plainLanguage: The generator and server use the same hash algorithm to create and check a 64-bit code. The user can enter the code in a form the server accepts.

sections.title: Generating a Sequence of Passwords
sections.content:
First, the generator combines the pass-phrase with a seed supplied in the server's challenge, hashes the result and folds it to 64 bits. The seed is not secret; it lets the same pass-phrase be used on different machines with different seeds and allows a sequence to be restarted with a changed seed.

The generator applies the hash function repeatedly to produce the password sequence. If the selected count is N, the first password is hashed N times, and the next is hashed N-1 times. After each successful authentication the count falls by one. An observer who sees one password cannot compute the next without reversing the hash function.

A text pass-phrase must contain at least 10 characters, and implementations must support pass-phrases from 10 to 63 characters. The seed must be alphanumeric, contain from 1 to 16 characters, and is converted to lower case before processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The server challenge supplies a seed and sequence count. Each login uses the next password in a hash sequence, and the count decreases after a successful login.

sections.title: Challenges and Human-Readable Codes
sections.content:
The challenge gives the algorithm identifier, sequence number and seed in a standard format: otp-<algorithm identifier> <sequence integer> <seed>. The RFC lists identifiers md4, md5 and sha1.

A 64-bit password may be represented as six words from a dictionary of 2048 words. The two extra bits in the six-word encoding carry a checksum. Generators must calculate that checksum, and servers must verify it. The RFC also requires servers to accept the hexadecimal format; they should accept the alternate dictionary format described in Appendix B.

Servers must accept the six-word format using the standard dictionary, without regard to case or spacing. The standard dictionary is included in the RFC and in RFC 1760.
sections.plainLanguage: The challenge tells the generator which algorithm, sequence step and seed to use. The resulting code can be written as hexadecimal or as six dictionary words for easier entry.

sections.title: Checking Passwords and Restarting the Sequence
sections.content:
The server stores the last successful one-time password for each user, or the initial password of a new sequence. To check a submitted password, the server decodes it to 64 bits, hashes it once and compares the result with the stored password. A match authenticates the user, and the submitted value becomes the stored value for the next check.

Because the sequence count decreases after each login, a user eventually needs to reinitialize. Implementations must provide a way to do this without revealing the pass-phrase, and must verify that the seed or pass-phrase changed. The RFC discourages sending the secret pass-phrase over a network in clear text.
sections.plainLanguage: The server remembers the last accepted code. It hashes the next code once and checks whether it matches that saved value.

sections.title: Race Attacks and Security Limits
sections.content:
A server must defend against a race attack. An attacker may hear most of a one-time password, guess the remaining part and try to finish authentication before the legitimate user. The RFC gives preventing simultaneous authentication sessions as one possible defense and says the defense needs a timeout to avoid denial of service.

OTP addresses passive eavesdropping and replay; it does not provide privacy for transmitted data and does not prevent active attacks such as session hijacking. The RFC recommends IPsec to protect against TCP session hijacking.

The system's security depends on the hash function. The RFC states that MD4 is generally believed to be weaker than MD5 and that a server supporting several algorithms is only as secure as its weakest supported algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: A one-time code can still be stolen in progress and raced against its owner. OTP also does not encrypt other data or stop an attacker who takes over an active session.
